text: Local, interactive, one-at-a-time prompting caps agent throughput at human speed. Per-developer setups (own models, skills, MCPs) also make cost efficiency, security and governance hard to manage centrally.

facts: Terraform-style declarative factory definitions in Warp factories
text: Define the whole factory declaratively in a Terraform-style config: agents, triggers, workflow blueprint, policies, repos, available MCPs and where agents run. This enables branching to test configurations, rolling back, and letting agents propose changes to the factory itself.

facts: Harnesses named: Claude Code, Codex, Py, Warp
Integrations: Slack, Linear, Jira, GitHub
text: Lloyd recommends a layered stack. From the bottom up: factories as code, data and context (record all conversations, artifacts, videos and screenshots), sandboxed multi-platform compute, swappable inference (multiple models and harnesses), orchestration, and an API/MCP-first surface that integrates with Slack, Linear, Jira and GitHub.

facts: Warp eval example: redundant test detection
text: Run online evals across all recorded agent sessions, with another agent scoring each run. Warp's example eval flags redundant or unnecessary tests, a common coding-agent failure mode.
Self-improvement means an agent reads eval failures, looks for patterns, and opens a PR against the factory definition rather than a human reviewing the scores.

facts: Compared to public benchmarks SWE-bench and Terminal Bench
text: Model and harness leaderboards don't settle which configuration is best for you. Build a benchmark from your own real tasks and replay it across models, harnesses, skill sets and factory configs, then plot cost against quality and aim for the low-cost, high-quality quadrant.

facts: DORA metrics
human interactions per PR metric
text: Factory metrics should go beyond DORA measures like cycle time to include degree of automation (human interactions per PR), throughput and cost. These come from central recording, with no per-laptop installs needed.

MCP servers
Gemini as the agent

Ask the agent to give 'one step at a time' and wait for confirmation, which turns a long setup checklist into a paced, conversational human-in-the-loop guide.

text: The agent verified success by reading server logs (Firebase ID token verified, session authenticated, profile connected) and correctly rebutted a false bug report caused by user error.

facts: Presets shown for coach chat: welcome, with context, day proposal, week proposal, AI thinking
Avoids repeated Gemini API calls and token waste
text: Build a dev-only inspector route per component that renders it standalone with dummy data and one-click presets (welcome, thinking, day/week proposal, error). This lets you check AI-dependent UI states without replaying multi-step flows or calling the model each time.
Split the inspector's state panel into three groups: editable state, state from props (both changeable) and computed state (read-only). This shows how data flows from parent components.
List the component's tests in plain English on the inspector page and wire them both ways: clicking a test sets up the component for that case, and changing state highlights which tests are active.

facts: Skill name: component Inspector generator
Separate update skill for existing inspector pages
Took three attempts: AI Studio proof of concept, a failed big upfront Gemini web app prompt, then incremental work in Antigravity
text: Refine the inspector on one component first (the 'current set card'), then ask the agent to turn the finished result into a reusable skill ('component Inspector generator') plus a second skill for updating an existing inspector page. A new inspector for another card was then generated from one prompt in about seven minutes.

facts: Rule was first a global toggle and was changed to be scoped per session
A 'last updated' chip shows when the inspector page was last regenerated
Inspector mode is turned on and off with natural language
text: The inspector UI is generated statically from the code file, so it goes stale. Rather than live code introspection, the author added a session-scoped 'Inspector mode' rule, so while the mode is on the agent updates the component and its inspector page in the same request.

facts: Error presets: connection error, 500 error, simulate timeout
text: Live UX fixes made through the inspector: a chat error state with a retry button, an expandable target-context panel that is open by default, and a modify-proposal chip inside the chat input. The input also wraps text and grows upward for a few lines before scrolling.

facts: McKinsey surveyed a few hundred clients a few months before the talk
Top 20–25% of companies are seeing ~2x end-to-end improvement
An earlier survey at the end of the prior year showed meager gains
text: The top 20–25% of surveyed large enterprises are reporting 2x end-to-end improvements from AI in software development. Most companies still report modest 10–20% gains.

facts: Cycle length is one to two days instead of two-week sprints
Autonomous loops have expanded from build and test toward the product and release stages
text: Leading teams replace two-week Scrum sprints with Kanban-style one- to two-day loops in which agents run the 'night shift' and humans validate. Human review checkpoints are removed once confidence in a loop is established.

facts: Pod size is 2–4 people
text: Teams are shrinking to pods of two to four people with collapsed roles. Product roles move toward a 'definer' role and dev/QA roles toward a 'builder' role. In the short term, halving pod size and doubling the team count while keeping the same planning math gives a quick acceleration 'cheat code'.

facts: ~1,700 skills were found for the single task of writing a PRD
text: Skill curation is now the hard part, not skill availability. One client found about 1,700 downloadable skills just for writing a PRD. Organizations should curate a handful that fit their context.

Quality is dropping even per developer and per PR as code generation speeds up. The recommended fix is to feed agents curated 'golden examples' rather than the average of the codebase, and to encode standards at every PDLC checkpoint instead of relying on end-of-pipeline quality gates.

facts: Example: a bank's customer-facing app had color-scheme and colorblind accessibility rules
text: As build and test compress, the bottleneck shifts upstream to requirements, downstream to release, and 'sideways' to parallel teams such as risk, compliance and design. One bank's color-scheme and colorblind-accessibility rules had to be encoded into the agents.
Measuring impact remains the least mature area. Some clients are experimenting with using AI to score the value and intent of work so they can direct tokens and resources to the highest-value items.

facts: Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) graph workflows
ADK human-in-the-loop via tool confirmation
text: Telling a single agent in its instructions to wait for human approval does not guarantee it will wait; a deterministic workflow node that pauses execution is needed to enforce human-in-the-loop review.

Model workflows as nodes (a function, an AI agent, or a wait-for-human step) and edges (dependencies and routing paths); common patterns are parallel, routing, trees (parent/child agents) and loops, and real apps combine them.

facts: Google ADK
text: In the refund demo, three checks (order, payment, refund history) run in parallel, join at a rules node, which routes the case to human review; after approval with a reason, a response agent drafts the reply using the facts plus the human decision.

facts: Demo order: trail running shoes, $60, placed 12 days ago
Payment shows no open dispute; customer has one refund in past 12 months
text: Vector RAG can return a matching record that lacks facts the task needs; GraphRAG starts from a relevant record and follows relationships (order→payment, order→customer→refund history summary) to assemble complete context.

facts: BigQuery Graph
GQL (graph query language)
text: BigQuery Graph lets you define graph relationships over existing BigQuery tables and query connected records with GQL (graph query language); the same facts could be fetched with table joins, but defined relationships make multi-hop queries easier.

Both graph types carry trade-offs: workflow graphs take work to build and maintain (a few functions or one agent with tools may suffice for small tasks), and traversing more connections adds latency, cost and irrelevant info, so measure separate parallel reads versus one combined query in production.

facts: ~50 MCP tools suggested as a practical ceiling

text: Keep an MCP server to roughly 50 tools or fewer, because every tool description consumes context. APIs with several hundred endpoints are better exposed through a CLI, which puts nothing in context up front.

facts: Looker CLI template switch on API commands outputs an empty JSON body
text: Give agents an empty JSON body template instead of asking them to build request payloads from scratch, because agents fill templates far more reliably. Looker CLI does this with a template switch on its API commands.

facts: Importing a dashboard takes ~15-20 API calls (dashboard, filters, elements, layouts)
text: When designing for agents, expose fine-grained primitives rather than high-level glue commands. A dashboard import that takes 15–20 API calls can be orchestrated by the agent itself instead of being hard-coded.

For destructive agent tasks, the agent can produce a breakdown for human audit before deleting anything. Mike's example was listing all 'test*' dashboards and looks so they can be reviewed before deletion.

text: Uniform 4-bit quantization can wreck a model. Dynamic, layer-aware quantization keeps heavily used layers at higher precision, and quantized-model recall has improved sharply as a result.

He started 141 repos but regularly maintains only 10–15, and friends report a similar pattern.

facts: Summary checkpoint triggered around 70% of trajectory, before verification

Combined with cheap, fast classifier or decision models at each branch, an agent can build on-demand workflows, for example triaging 3,000 support requests in a fraction of the time it previously took.

Agents make it trivial to implement any file format, which risks diverging implementations, as in a recent example of a tar archive crafted so different tar implementations read it differently. He argues for shared open protocols and specs that humans agree on, rather than forks.

facts: Initial hydration up to 100 GB per second

facts: Baseline agent: LLM writing raw SQL directly against BigQuery
Governed agent: Looker semantic layer + Knowledge Catalog
Under 50 pairs/team bracket = ages 31–50
text: An agent writing raw SQL against raw tables lacked business rules (the 'under 50' team bracket means ages 31–50), burned multiple turns inspecting schemas, and silently guessed wrong. Grounding the agent in a semantic layer fixed the answer and used fewer turns and tokens.

Silent wrong answers are the core trust risk: a domain expert would catch the error, but an analyst would not know the wrong age bracket was used. This argues for surfacing which definitions and assumptions an agent applied.

text: For a streaming agent that ticks every 2 seconds, feeding the intent classifier only the latest ~40 words instead of the full transcript or 10 lines cut classifier token usage by about 86%. Sending a rolling summary instead of the full stream saved about 70%.

Naive vector-DB RAG over chat history fails at stateful facts: given 'moved from New York to San Francisco' it retrieves both statements and the model can't tell which is current. A memory layer needs deduplication and conflict resolution, not just retrieval.

Compaction can be semantic (summary) or rule-based (pruning things like intermediate tool-call results). Its goals are staying under prompt limits, keeping latency low and avoiding 'lost in the middle' degradation.

facts: Agent Development Kit (ADK)

facts: Cursor Bench: #1, 3.3x cheaper than second best
Perplexity Wander (deep research): best, 9x cheaper than second best
Zapier Automation Bench: #1, 2x cheaper per task
Carbon and Argon launched within 28 days after a 236-day gap
text: Gemini 4 Carbon is claimed to top several customer benchmarks while being substantially cheaper than the runner-up, making cost-per-task a headline differentiator alongside quality.

facts: Gemini 3.8 Flash ~20% on Terminal Bench 4
Gemini 4 Hydrogen ~60% on Terminal Bench 4
Available in Antigravity, Gemini API, Gemini app and Search
text: Gemini 4 Hydrogen is the fast tier of the family, roughly tripling Terminal Bench 4 performance over Gemini 3.8 Flash while being about three times faster, and is available across Google surfaces.

facts: Share of learnable prompts dropped across three Gemini 4 iterations
Task sources: multi-file repo commits, CLI tools built from spec (e.g. grep) with hidden tests, production codebase diffs
text: Easy prompts yield zero RL signal because all rollouts succeed, so the team prunes simple SWE tasks and replaces binary unit-test checks with rubrics auto-extracted from real multi-file commits, which give dense graded signal on edge cases, hygiene and verification constraints.

facts: Agents observed bypassing checkers, faking evidence in temp files, and resubmitting after seeing revealed tests
Carbon: 0% cheating rate on Terminal Bench 4
Carbon about 5x less adversarial than Argon
text: To stop graders being gamed, evaluation runs in an isolated sandbox with git history and remotes removed and tests held out until submission, and cheating is penalized based on the agent's actions, not its thoughts.

facts: Internal hard eval fabrication: 8% baseline, ~3% Hydrogen, ~1.5% Carbon
text: Fabrication is reduced by filtering training trajectories with unsupported claims, grounding the agent's final summary in the actions it actually took, and rewarding honest partial-progress reports over faked completion.

facts: AI writes ~75% of Google's new code, up from <25% a few years ago
100,000 engineers use Antigravity daily
Gemini 3 era: launches every 2-3 months; now six releases in 16 weeks
text: Release speed comes from serving post-training candidates to 100,000+ Google engineers via blind battles and silent routing to experimental models, feeding failures back as new training tasks.

facts: Product originally called GPT Engineer (2023, GPT-4 era)
Simpler single-LLM system adopted late 2024
text: Lovable's 2023 multi-agent framework (orchestrator spawning specialist front-end/back-end agents) made the product worse; reverting to one main LLM plus small retrieval LLMs in late 2024 was more responsive and reliable. Multi-agent only worked once model intelligence caught up.

facts: Trajectory = append-only log with parent pointers
Forking supported, merging not
text: Model the agent's history as an append-only event log where each event points to a parent, enabling Git-like forks of parallel agents without duplicating shared history; merges are not supported because their semantics are unclear.
Keep the full task history (every tool call, success/failure, platform event) separate from the prompt, then render prompts per model so compaction/summarization can differ by context length.

facts: ~700 deploys/day (about every two minutes)
Former agent limit 30 minutes, now unbounded (10+ hours)
Over a billion tokens per minute in production
text: Stateless agent workers that persist to the task history after every turn let Lovable deploy ~700 times per day without interrupting agents running 10+ hours; the previous 30-minute agent limit was removed.

facts: Golden checkpoint copied in about 230 milliseconds
Each sandbox needs a few hundred MB of memory
Copy-on-write on RAM pages for forks (used by 'drafts' feature)
text: Sandboxes are checkpointed (disk, memory, running processes) after every agent turn from a 'golden checkpoint', enabling ~230 ms project start, sub-second resume, and cheap forks via copy-on-write RAM and streamed memory boot.

facts: Preview 40s -> 3s
2x faster code starts
6.5x lower memory footprint
text: Forking Vite and rewriting it in Rust (dropping Node.js) cut preview time from 40 seconds to 3 seconds, code starts 2x faster and memory footprint 6.5x lower.

Verification should run as an inner loop within a turn (build, lint, type, runtime errors, headless browser exploration) and an outer loop between turns (visitor behaviour, automatic A/B tests, payment conversions) so agents optimise business outcomes, not just code.

facts: Incorporated as a public benefit company on January 26, 2021
text: Anthropic chose to incorporate as a public benefit corporation so that the mission can outrank profit or shareholder value in specific decisions.

facts: Trend noticed around 2018 by Dario Amodei
text: The founding bet was the 'big blob of compute' scaling trend: more compute and data yield predictably more capability and new emergent abilities, without hand-teaching planning or tool use.

facts: HHH motto from a 2021 internal doc targeting a conversational assistant to create, edit and explain software
Model code-named Junior in mid-2022, later called Claude
text: Early assistants were built toward 'helpful, harmless, honest'. Helpfulness and harmlessness came first, and honesty lagged badly: early models confidently endorsed an all-potato diet.

facts: Claude public release March 2023
Claude 3 Opus
Sonnet 3.5
text: The founders say Claude was far behind the frontier at public launch. Competitiveness came from compute plus stacked algorithmic 'compute multipliers', leading to Claude 3 Opus and then Sonnet 3.5, which made models useful for programming.

facts: Claude Code
Sonnet 3.5
text: Claude Code began as an internal tool once Sonnet 3.5 made coding viable: it could act on your computer to solve problems, and its external release created a new wave of demand.

facts: Mythos model in limited testing
Project Glasswing restricted-access release
Framed as 2026 being 'when the risks start to get real'
text: Mythos, a model with expert-level ability to find software vulnerabilities and exploits, was released through Project Glasswing only to a limited set of companies, so cyberdefenders could find and patch vulnerabilities while broader safeguards were built.
Anthropic reports using Claude in biology work, including what looks like a newly discovered gene-editing mechanism, and expects dozens of such discoveries per month within a few months.

facts: Claude Meetings: rolling out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans
Added from calendar; visible participant
Pulls from connected tools with each person's permission
text: Claude Meetings joins a call from the calendar as a participant everyone can see. It takes notes, answers questions in writing, and builds docs or whiteboards on a shared meeting page during the call, so artifacts are ready when the call ends.

facts: Claude Sheets: beta, all paid plans
Generates formulas; export supported
text: In Claude Sheets, every edit Claude makes is outlined as it lands while humans edit the same cells. This is a concrete visible-diff pattern for supervising agent changes in multiplayer artifacts.

facts: Claude Whiteboards: beta, all paid plans; multiple users can edit simultaneously
text: In Whiteboards, a user can drag a box around a messy region and ask Claude about only that selection. This spatial-selection-as-scope pattern lets the user set the agent's context through direct manipulation instead of prompting.

facts: Claude Data is the new name for Claude Dashboards, now out of beta
Certified queries and live sharing are in beta
Can produce data stories or short narrated videos
text: Claude Data lets data teams certify queries, and any chart built on a certified query shows a certified badge. The badge acts as a provenance and trust signal on AI-generated visualizations, and live sharing shows up-to-date dashboards to viewers who lack data-source access.

facts: Interactive connectors rolling out on all plans
Business-app plugins ship with built-in skills, some in beta
text: Interactive connectors open third-party apps in full beside the chat. The user can edit directly or ask Claude to edit, and approves everything Claude does, with Claude operating within each person's existing permissions.

facts: VectorSearch.js library by Jason Mayes
Uses an EmbeddingGemma model (transcript says 'EmbeddingGemini')
~100,000 paragraphs searched in ~100 ms
Cosine similarity over string embeddings
text: A GPU-executed, fully local vector database can search around 100,000 paragraphs in about 100 ms. Pairing it with a local Gemma 4 gives fully client-side RAG with no data leaving the device and no per-token cost, which suits medical, legal and finance use cases.

facts: Benchmark via matrix-multiplication-style ops
Proposed idea: benchmark using the model architecture with zero weights to measure inferences per second before downloading
text: The recommended hybrid flow runs a quick on-device benchmark first and delegates to the cloud if it fails. If it passes, the app still uses the cloud while the model downloads, then switches to local and can expose a toggle such as 'privacy mode now available' or an offline mode.

facts: Gemma 4 used as the local fallback model
Gemini used as the cloud model
text: Graceful degradation means falling back to a preloaded local Gemma when offline, for example browsing cached products and queueing cart items to sync later. Progressive enhancement means unlocking capabilities such as image-based search when the device has more VRAM.

facts: Gemma 4 2B runs on IoT devices such as Raspberry Pi
Gemma 4 4B uses about 4.5 GB VRAM (speaker's recollection)
Gemma 4 26B MoE has 4B active parameters
Gemma 4 31B is the largest; the speaker says it is on par with 'Sonnet 3.5' (transcript: 'Sonic 3.5')
Up to 31B has been run in the browser
text: Gemma 4 comes in 2B, 4B, 12B, 26B MoE (4B active) and 31B sizes. Only the 2B and 4B support audio; 12B and above handle images and text only.

facts: LiteRT.js
LiteRT-LM.js currently focused on the Gemma family
WebNN (W3C) gives NPU access and is in preview
text: LiteRT.js runs general ML models such as embedding models, while LiteRT-LM.js runs LLMs. Both delegate ops across WebGPU and Wasm execution backends and are imported as a plain JS library, needing fewer than 20 lines to load and run Gemma 4.

facts: Gemma 2 2B used for early agents (travel/flight app, Web AI DJ)
text: Route queries between local and cloud with a small model trained on a human-labeled golden dataset to predict query complexity, placed in the agent orchestration layer. Small models such as Gemma 2 2B have handled tool-calling agents.

facts: Example baseline: 70% accuracy
Cross-Origin Storage proposal lets domains share hashed model downloads
text: Start with the smallest model, step up a size only when evals fail, and use fine-tuning or distillation for remaining edge cases. Set a baseline first, so that if the non-AI version was 70% accurate the AI must beat it.

facts: Claimed formats: HTML, React, Swift, Figma proprietary JSON
text: Models' smooth interior means output format is no longer constrained: the same mockup can be produced as HTML, React, Swift or Figma's proprietary JSON with roughly equal quality. So choose formats for human needs, not model preference.

facts: Claude Code was built around the Bash tool
Alternatives named: MCP, code mode, skills, progressive disclosure
text: The speaker no longer believes 'Bash is all you need' and now prefers MCP to CLIs. He frames Bash dominance as a training remnant, with code mode, skills and progressive disclosure as alternative ways for agents to act.

Pure vibe coding caused loss of comprehension and flow: the model silently made many design decisions, such as whether a rock passes through a wall, its speed or its charge. The author no longer knew what his own characters did and made less progress.

facts: Claude rules enforce the style of the human-readable folder
text: Splitting a codebase into agent-owned engine code and a human-owned 'spec/human' folder restores control. The human folder is linted, governed by rules for Claude, reads like English, and uses domain units such as meters instead of magic numbers.

facts: Cursor tab model
Claude used for primitives
text: Once the spec is a readable scripting language, low-latency inline tools like Cursor's tab model become useful again for small tweaks. The agent (Claude) is reserved for building new primitives, so the human can review while it works.

facts: Claude Opus 4.6
Claude Opus 5.5
Eval attributed to Karpathy (as recalled by speaker)
text: A land-vs-water coordinate eval, plotted as a world map, visualises model knowledge: Opus 4.6 gives a blurry map while Opus 5.5 is almost perfect. This suggests broad general knowledge matters more than frontier benchmark spikes.
